do.e: From Middle English don, from Old English dōn, from Proto-West Germanic *dōn, from Proto-Germanic *dōną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, do, make”). For senses 4 and 5, compare Old Norse duga, also Northern English dow. The past tense form is from Middle English didde, dude.

doctor.e: From Middle English doctor, doctour (“an expert, authority on a subject”), from Anglo-Norman doctour, from Latin doctor (“teacher”), from doceō (“to teach”).
doctor.g: A physician; a member of the medical profession; one who is trained and licensed to heal the sick or injured. The final examination and qual

doctrine.e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin doctrina (“teaching, instruction, learning, knowledge”), from doctor (“a teacher”), from docere (“to teach”); see doctor.
doctrine.g: A belief or tenet, especially about philosophical or theological matters.

document.e: Borrowed from Middle French document, from Latin documentum.
document.g: An original or official paper used as the basis, proof, or support of anything else, including any writing, book, or other instrument convey

doe.e: From Middle English do (“(female) fallow deer”), from Old English dā, from Proto-West Germanic *daihā (“female deer, mother deer”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck (milk), to suckle”). Related also to female, filial, fetus.
doe.g: A female deer; also used of similar animals such as antelope (less commonly a goat, as nanny is also used).

doer.e: From Middle English doer, doar, doere, from Old English dōere (“a doer; worker”), equivalent to do + -er.
doer.g: Someone who does, performs, or executes; an active person, an agent.

dog.e: From Middle English dogge (akin to Scots dug), from Old English docga, *dogga, of uncertain origin. The original meaning seems to have been a common dog, as opposed to a well-bred one, or something like 'cur', and perhaps later came to be used for stocky dogs.
dog.g: A mammal of the family Canidae:

doing.g: The sound made by an elastic object when struck by or striking a hard object.

dole.e: From Middle English dol, from Old English dāl (“portion, share, division, allotment”), from Proto-Germanic *dailą (“part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰayl- (“part, watershed”).
From Middle English dole (“grief”), from Old French doel (compare French deuil), from Late Latin dolus, from Latin doleo.

doleful.e: From Middle English doleful, doolful, deolful, equivalent to dole + -ful.
doleful.g: Filled with grief, mournful, bringing feelings of sadness.

domain.e: From Middle English demayne, demain (“rule”), from Old French demeine, demaine, demeigne, domaine (“power”), (French domaine), from Latin dominium (“property, right of ownership”), from dominus (“master, proprietor, owner”).
domain.g: A geographic area owned or controlled by a single person or organization.

dominate.e: Borrowed from Latin dominātus, perfect active participle of dominor (“to rule, have dominion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dominus (“lord, master”) + -or (verb-forming suffix).
dominate.g: To govern, rule or control by superior authority or power.

dominate.e: Ultimately from Latin dominor (“rule, have dominion”), either from Latin dominātus, the perfect active participle of dominor (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), or via phonetic alteration of the synonym dominant, from Latin domināns, the present active participle of the same.

dominion.e: From Middle English dominion, from Middle French dominion, from Latin dominium (“lordship, right of ownership”), from dominus (“lord”), from domus (“house”).
dominion.g: Power or the use of power; sovereignty over something; stewardship, supremacy.

don.e: From Latin dominus (“lord, head of household”), akin to Italian don, Sicilian don, Spanish don; from domus (“house”).
don.g: A university professor, particularly one at Oxford or Cambridge.

don.e: From Middle English don (“to put on”), from Old English dōn on; equivalent to do + on.
don.g: To put on clothing; to dress (oneself) in an article of personal attire.

don't.e: From do + -n't. Depending on dialect, its use in the third-person singular may be from elision (in these dialects does is used when not in the negative) or from not using -s to mark the third-person singular at all.

donation.e: From Middle English donacion, donation, from Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiō (“a present”), from dōnō (“to give”), from dōnum (“a gift”). Recorded in English since the 15th century. Equivalent to donate + -ion.
donation.g: A voluntary gift or contribution for a specific cause.

done.e: From Middle English don, idon, ydon, ȝedon, gedon, from Old English dōn, ġedōn, from Proto-West Germanic *dān, from Proto-Germanic *dēnaz (past participle of *dōną (“to do”)). Equivalent to do + -en (past participle ending).
done.g: Having completed or finished an activity.

donkey.e: The origin is uncertain. Originally a slang term from the late eighteenth century. Perhaps from Middle English *donekie (“a miniature dun horse”), a double diminutive of Middle English don, dun, dunne (a name for a dun horse), equivalent to modern English dun (“brownish grey colour”) + -ock (diminutive suffix) + -ie (diminutive suffix).
donkey.g: A domestic animal, Equus asinus asinus, similar to a horse.

doom.e: From Middle English doom, dom, from Old English dōm (“judgement”), from Proto-West Germanic *dōm, from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰóh₁mos.

door.e: From Middle English dore, dor, from Old English duru (“door”), dor (“gate”), from Proto-West Germanic *dur, from Proto-Germanic *durz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwṓr, from *dʰwer- (“doorway, door, gate”). Despite.
door.g: A portal of entry into a building, room, or vehicle, typically consisting of a rigid plane movable on a hinge. It may have a handle to help

doorframe.g: The frame into which a door is fitted.

doorkeeper.g: The person in charge of an entryway, sometimes responsible for security in the immediate area around the entryway.

doorpost.g: Either of the upright posts on either side of a door, which together support a lintel; a doorjamb.

doorway.g: The passage of a door; a door-shaped entrance into a house or a room.

dor.e: From Middle English dorre, dore, from Old English dora (“humming insect”), from Proto-West Germanic *dorō, from Proto-Germanic *durô (“bumblebee, humming insect”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-, *dʰreh₁n- (“bee, hornet, drone”).
dor.g: Any of species Geotrupes stercorarius of large European dung beetles that make a droning noise while flying.

dote.e: The noun in the sense of "imbecile" is derived from Middle English dote (“simpleton”), itself from doten (see above). The noun in the sense of "darling" and "decay" is derived from the modern verb.
dote.g: To be weakly or foolishly fond of somebody.

dote.e: From Middle English dote (“endowment”) (c. 1450), from Middle French dote (modern dot), from Latin dos.

doting.e: From Middle English dotynge; equivalent to dote + -ing.
doting.g: Characterized by giving love and affection.

double.e: From Middle English double, from Old French doble, double, from Latin duplus (“twofold”).
double.g: Made up of two matching or complementary elements.

double-minded.g: Of two minds; indecisive, vacillating, or ambivalent.

double-tongued.e: From Middle English doubultongud, dowbyl townged, dubble tungyd, equivalent to double + tongued.
double-tongued.g: Saying one thing to one person and something different to another; double talking; deceitful in speech.

doubly.e: From Middle English dowbly, doubli, dubli, doubeliche, equivalent to double + -ly.
doubly.g: In a double manner; with twice the severity or degree.

doubt.e: Spelling reformers of the early modern period added the letter b to reflect the Latin root dubitō, but it has never been pronounced in English.
doubt.g: To consider questionable or unlikely; to hesitate to believe; to lack confidence in; to question.

doubtful.e: From Middle English doutfull, douteful, equivalent to doubt + -ful.

doubtless.e: From Middle English douteles, dowteles, equivalent to doubt + -less.
doubtless.g: Characterized by or experiencing no doubt at all, certain; undoubted; undoubting.

dough.e: From Middle English dow, dogh, dagh, from Old English dāg, from Proto-Germanic *daigaz (“dough”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead, form, mold”). The derivation of the second meaning (of money) is obscure, but dates to the mid 19th century.
dough.g: A thick, malleable substance made by mixing flour with other ingredients such as water, eggs, or butter, that is made into a particular form

dove.e: A modern formation of the strong conjugation, by analogy with drive → drove and weave → wove.

down.e: From Middle English doun, doune (“down”), from Old English dūne (“down”), aphetic form of adūne (“down, downward”), from earlier ofdūne (“down”, literally “off the hill”), from of (“of, off of”) + dūn (“hill, mount, dune, down”).
down.g: From a higher position to a lower one; downwards.

down.e: From Middle English doune, from Old English dūn, from Proto-West Germanic *dūn (“sandhill, dune”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *dūnaz, *dūnǭ (“pile, heap”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze, dust”). Alternatively, perhaps borrowed from Proto-Celtic *dūnom (“hill.
down.g: A hill; in England, especially a chalk hill.

downcast.e: The English word is analysable as down- (prefix meaning ‘lower direction or position’) + cast (“that has been thrown”, adjective).
downcast.g: Of the eyes, a facial expression, etc.: looking downwards, usually as a sign of discouragement, sadness, etc., or sometimes modesty.

downcast.e: From Middle English downcast (“misfortune”), adoun-cast (“destruction, overthrow”), from adoun (“downward”) + cast (“a throw, a cast”) (from Old Norse kast (“a throw”), from kasten (“to cast, throw”)), from Middle English casten adoun: see etymology 1.
downcast.g: An act of looking downwards, usually as a sign of discouragement, sadness, etc., or sometimes modesty; hence (uncountable, archaic), dejecti

downfall.e: From down- + fall. In this spelling, from 16th century; spelled as two words from 13th century.
downfall.g: A precipitous decline in fortune; death or rapid deterioration, as in status or wealth.

downsitting.g: The act of sitting down; repose, sitting or resting.

dowry.e: From Middle English dowarye, dowerie, from Anglo-Norman dowarie, douarie, from Old French douaire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs.
dowry.g: Payment, such as property or money, paid by the bride's family to the groom or his family at the time of marriage.
